title: Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co. v. Owens (2014)
summary: The removal notice could allege the required amount without attaching proof; a contested amount required a later evidentiary determination.
notes:
The opinion’s discussion of CAFA does not automatically decide every presumption for ordinary removal. The casebook revisits this decision in the class-action jurisdiction material at pages 871–872.

Facts and posture: Owens filed a Kansas state-court class action over underpaid oil-and-gas royalties; Dart's CAFA removal notice alleged more than $8 million in controversy without evidence; the district court remanded under Tenth Circuit precedent, the Tenth Circuit denied leave to appeal the remand, and the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J.) held that denial an abuse of discretion, vacated and remanded.

The Court also stated that no antiremoval presumption attends cases invoking CAFA, and that when the amount is contested the removing defendant must establish it by a preponderance of the evidence under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(c)(2)(B).

The decision was 5–4: Justice Scalia dissented (joined by Justices Kennedy and Kagan, and by Justice Thomas in part) on the ground that the Court could review only the Tenth Circuit's discretionary refusal to hear the appeal, and Justice Thomas dissented separately.

sections.Parties: Dart Cherokee removed a class action brought by Owens and asserted that the amount in controversy satisfied CAFA.
sections.Material Facts: The removing defendant stated the amount in its notice but did not include the evidentiary submission demanded by the lower court. The issue concerned the notice’s initial sufficiency and the procedure for resolving a later dispute over the amount.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected the requirement that the removal notice itself contain evidence proving the jurisdictional amount.
sections.Issue: Must a removing defendant attach proof of the amount in controversy to the initial notice of removal?
sections.Holding: No. A plausible allegation suffices initially. When contested by the plaintiff or questioned by the court, the parties submit proof and the court determines the amount under the applicable evidentiary standard.
sections.Reasoning: The removal statute called for a short and plain statement, which the Court did not equate with a full evidentiary presentation. Pleading the jurisdictional amount and proving it after a genuine dispute are distinct procedural stages. The Court also declined to apply an anti-removal presumption to CAFA, whose design expanded federal access for the covered class actions.

learning.why: The removal notice could allege the required amount without attaching proof; a contested amount required a later evidentiary determination.

topics.cp-removal: A notice of removal needed a plausible allegation of the jurisdictional amount; evidentiary proof was required when the allegation was contested.
topics.cp-cafa: The Court rejected an anti-removal presumption in the CAFA setting.
topics.cp-amount-in-controversy: When disputed, the amount was determined from evidence under the preponderance standard described in the note.
topics.cp-usc-1453: The appeal reached the Court through § 1453(c)'s discretionary review of CAFA remand orders, and the holding governs CAFA removal pleading.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: The Court rejected any antiremoval presumption for CAFA cases and read § 1446(a) by analogy to Rule 8(a) pleading.

mnemonic.rationale: Royalties and a CAFA removal notice
